Methods behind the new features: formulas, code and rationale

Source: vignettes/articles/methods.Rmd
methods.Rmd

Each new way of estimating weights added since ipw 1.3.2 comes down to the same step: estimate the probability, or density, of the exposure each person actually received, then take a ratio. This article gives, for each new feature, the formula, the code in the package and why that approach was chosen. Section 6 covers recurrent exposure events (Graffeo et al. 2018), section 7 ipwprobtm(), which turns probabilities you estimated yourself into time-varying weights, and section 8 the standard errors of ipwvcov() (experimental). How to use the features is shown in the main vignette; whether they recover known effects is checked in the simulation study.

Notation and the shared formula

Every family only has to supply f, the probability or density of the observed exposure; the weight formula itself is the same for all of them.

  • A: the exposure each person received; L: confounders in the denominator model; V: covariates in the numerator model (often none).
  • f(a | ·): the probability of a for a discrete exposure, the density of a for a continuous one.

Point treatment, stabilized and unstabilized:

SWi=f(Ai∣Vi)f(Ai∣Li),Wi=1f(Ai∣Li) SW_i = \frac{f(A_i \mid V_i)}{f(A_i \mid L_i)}, \qquad W_i = \frac{1}{f(A_i \mid L_i)}

Time-varying, for subject i at time t, with A‾\bar{A} and L‾\bar{L} the history up to that interval:

SWi(t)=∏k≤tf(Aik∣A‾i,k−1,Vi)f(Aik∣A‾i,k−1,L‾ik) SW_i(t) = \prod_{k \le t} \frac{f(A_{ik} \mid \bar{A}_{i,k-1}, V_i)}{f(A_{ik} \mid \bar{A}_{i,k-1}, \bar{L}_{ik})}

In ipwpoint(), each family’s branch returns dens for the numerator and denominator models, and one line forms the weight:

ipw_weights <- num$dens / den$dens   # num$dens = 1 when numerator = NULL

1. estimand: ATT, ATC and overlap weights for a binomial point treatment

The estimand argument changes which population the weights standardise to, using the same fitted propensity score e(L) = P(A = 1 | L) from the denominator model.

Formula.

ATE: w=Ae+1−A1−eATT: w=A+(1−A)e1−eATC: w=A1−ee+(1−A)ATO: w=A(1−e)+(1−A)e \text{ATE: } w = \frac{A}{e} + \frac{1-A}{1-e} \qquad \text{ATT: } w = A + (1-A)\frac{e}{1-e} \qquad \text{ATC: } w = A\frac{1-e}{e} + (1-A) \qquad \text{ATO: } w = A(1-e) + (1-A)\,e

Code.

ipw_weights <- switch(estimand,
  ATE = num$dens / den$dens,
  ATT = ifelse(exp_vec == 1, 1, den$p / (1 - den$p)),
  ATC = ifelse(exp_vec == 1, (1 - den$p) / den$p, 1),
  ATO = ifelse(exp_vec == 1, 1 - den$p, den$p)
)

den$p is the fitted P(A = 1 | L) kept from the binomial denominator model; "ATT", "ATC" and "ATO" require numerator = NULL.

Why this approach. Each estimand answers a different clinical question; the formulas only change who gets how much weight.

  • ATE (default): “What would happen if everyone were treated, compared with no one?” Each person is weighted to stand for the whole study population.
  • ATT: “Did the treatment help the people who actually received it?” Treated people keep weight 1; untreated people are reweighted to look like the treated group. Useful when treatment is only realistic for some patients.
  • ATC: “What would the treatment have done for the people who did not receive it?” The mirror image of the ATT: untreated people keep weight 1 and treated people are reweighted to look like the untreated group. Useful when the question is whether to extend a treatment to those not yet receiving it.
  • ATO (overlap): “What is the effect in patients for whom doctors could have gone either way?” Every weight lies between 0 and 1, so no single person can dominate. This helps when some patients are almost always or almost never treated: there, ATE weights become huge and need truncation. With a logistic model, overlap weights also make the average of every covariate in the model exactly equal between the groups.
  • Why no numerator: ATT, ATC and overlap weights are not a ratio of two probabilities, so stabilizing them has no meaning. ipw gives an error instead of silently ignoring a numerator.
  • Which to use: choose by the clinical question first. If ATE weights are extreme, consider ATO, and state clearly which patients the result describes.

Caveat. The overlap population is defined by the propensity score itself, so results describe that population, not a pre-specified one; this should be stated when reporting ATO estimates.

ATT and overlap weights for multinomial and ordinal exposures

For an exposure with levels k=1,…,Kk = 1, \dots, K, let Pi(k)P_i(k) be the fitted probability of level kk for person i (from nnet::multinom or MASS::polr) and AiA_i the observed level.

Formula. With a focal level ff (argument focal), and for generalized overlap weights (Li & Li 2019):

ATT: wi=Pi(f)Pi(Ai)ATO: wi=1/Pi(Ai)∑k=1K1/Pi(k) \text{ATT: } w_i = \frac{P_i(f)}{P_i(A_i)} \qquad \text{ATO: } w_i = \frac{1 / P_i(A_i)}{\sum_{k=1}^{K} 1 / P_i(k)}

People at the focal level get ATT weight 1. With K=2K = 2, Pi(2)=eP_i(2) = e and f=2f = 2 these are the binomial formulas above: ATT gives e/(1−e)e/(1-e) to the others, and ATO gives (1/e)/(1/e+1/(1−e))=1−e(1/e) / (1/e + 1/(1-e)) = 1 - e to level 2 and ee to level 1.

Code. The full matrix of fitted probabilities is built by the internal helper .prob_matrix() (also used for the probability of the observed level):

ipw_weights <- switch(estimand,
  ATT = ifelse(as.character(exp_vec) == focal, 1, den$pmat[, focal] / den$dens),
  ATO = (1 / den$dens) / rowSums(1 / den$pmat)
)

Why this approach. The ATT for a categorical exposure compares every level with what would have happened to the people at the focal level, so the weights reweight each other level to resemble the focal group. The generalized overlap weights target the people with substantial probability of every level; like binomial overlap weights they are bounded, here by 1. "ATC" is not offered for categorical exposures: with more than two levels there is no single control group, and the effect in the controls is the ATT with focal set to the control level.

2. Skewed continuous exposures: "gamma" and "lognormal"

For a positive, right-skewed exposure (dose, duration, a biomarker), f is a gamma or log-normal density instead of a normal one.

Formula. Gamma with log link, mean μi = exp(Liᵀβ) and shape k = 1/φ, where φ is the dispersion estimated by the GLM:

f(a∣L)=(k/μ)kΓ(k)ak−1e−ka/μ f(a \mid L) = \frac{(k/\mu)^{k}}{\Gamma(k)}\, a^{k-1} e^{-k a / \mu}

Log-normal: a normal linear model for log A with mean μi = Liᵀβ and standard deviation σ:

f(a∣L)=1aσ2πexp⁡(−(log⁡a−μ)22σ2) f(a \mid L) = \frac{1}{a \sigma \sqrt{2\pi}} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(\log a - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right)

The factor 1/a is the same in numerator and denominator, so the stabilized log-normal weight equals the gaussian weight computed on log A.

Code.

# gamma
mod   <- do.call(stats::glm, c(base, list(family = stats::Gamma(link = "log")), dots))
shape <- 1 / summary(mod)$dispersion
mu    <- as.numeric(stats::predict(mod, type = "response"))
dens  <- stats::dgamma(exp_vec, shape = shape, rate = shape / mu)

# lognormal: the model formula is log(exposure) ~ ...
mod  <- do.call(stats::glm, c(base, list(family = stats::gaussian()), dots))
dens <- stats::dlnorm(exp_vec, meanlog = as.numeric(stats::predict(mod)),
                      sdlog = stats::sd(stats::residuals(mod)))

The exposure must be positive, and a numerator model is required.

Why this approach.

  • The problem: doses, durations and many lab values are always positive and have a long right tail: most values are small, a few are very large. The normal model is symmetric and allows negative values, so it fits the tails badly, and the tails are where the weights are largest.
  • Gamma: suits exposures whose spread grows with their size, for example a duration that varies by about 20% whatever its typical length. Common for durations, doses and costs.
  • Log-normal: suits exposures that look bell-shaped after taking the log, such as viral load and many biomarkers. In practice it is the gaussian model applied to log(exposure).
  • Which to use: draw a histogram of log(exposure). If it looks bell-shaped, use log-normal; otherwise try gamma. You can also compare the AIC of the two denominator models.
  • Why the numerator is required: for a continuous exposure, f is a density, not a probability. Its size depends on the units (mg or g), so 1/f has no fixed meaning and can be huge. Dividing by a numerator density, as already required for gaussian, cancels the units and keeps the weights around 1.

Implementation notes. The gamma shape uses the moment (Pearson) estimate of φ from summary.glm(), not maximum likelihood (MASS::gamma.shape() would be the alternative). The log-normal σ uses sd() of the residuals (divisor n − 1, not n − p), to match the existing gaussian family.

Caveat. In the simulation study a small bias (4–6%) remained with the correct family. Weights computed from the true densities had the same bias, so it is a property of weighting with a skewed exposure in finite samples, and it shrinks slowly as the sample grows.

3. Count exposures: "poisson" and "negbin"

For a count exposure (number of doses, visits), f is the probability mass of the observed count, from a log-linear model for its mean.

Formula. Both models have a log link, μi = exp(Liᵀβ). Poisson, then negative binomial with dispersion parameter θ (variance μ + μ²/θ):

f(a∣L)=e−μμaa! f(a \mid L) = \frac{e^{-\mu} \mu^{a}}{a!}

f(a∣L)=Γ(a+θ)Γ(θ)a!(θθ+μ)θ(μθ+μ)a f(a \mid L) = \frac{\Gamma(a + \theta)}{\Gamma(\theta)\, a!} \left(\frac{\theta}{\theta + \mu}\right)^{\theta} \left(\frac{\mu}{\theta + \mu}\right)^{a}

Code.

# poisson
mod  <- .fit_glm_or_gam(c(base, list(family = stats::poisson()), dots))
dens <- stats::dpois(exp_vec, lambda = as.numeric(stats::predict(mod, type = "response")))

# negbin: theta estimated by glm.nb, separately for numerator and denominator
mod  <- do.call(MASS::glm.nb, c(base, dots))
dens <- stats::dnbinom(exp_vec, size = mod$theta,
                       mu = as.numeric(stats::predict(mod, type = "response")))

The exposure must be a non-negative integer.

Why this approach.

  • The problem: a count (number of doses: 0, 1, 2, …) is neither yes/no nor a smooth measurement. A normal model allows impossible values such as −1.3 doses and gives poor probabilities for large counts, which is exactly where weights become large.
  • Poisson: the standard model for counts. It assumes the spread of the counts equals their average.
  • Negative binomial: real counts often vary more than that: many patients get no doses and a few get very many. A Poisson model then gives too small a chance to these unusual counts, and so too large a weight. The negative binomial adds one parameter for the extra spread.
  • Which to use: start with Poisson; if the variance of the exposure is clearly larger than its mean, use the negative binomial. In the simulation study, the negative binomial also worked for Poisson counts (bias 3.0%), while Poisson weights for overdispersed counts were badly biased.
  • Why the numerator is optional: for counts, f is a true probability between 0 and 1, as for a yes/no exposure, so unstabilized weights 1/f still make sense.

Caveat. Zero-inflated or truncated counts are not covered.

4. Smooth terms with mgcv

When a formula contains s(), te(), ti() or t2(), the exposure model is fitted as a generalized additive model, so a confounder’s effect can be nonlinear without hand-built splines.

Formula. With link g and smooth functions fj represented by penalized regression splines:

g(E[A∣L])=β0+∑jfj(Lj)+Llin⊤γ g\big(E[A \mid L]\big) = \beta_0 + \sum_j f_j(L_j) + L_{\text{lin}}^\top \gamma

Each fj is fitted by minimising the penalized deviance below; λj sets its smoothness and is estimated by mgcv (default method = "GCV.Cp"; method = "REML" can be passed through ...).

D(β)+∑jλj∫fj″(x)2dx D(\beta) + \sum_j \lambda_j \int f_j''(x)^2 \, dx

The weights then follow the notation section, with f taken from the GAM’s fitted values.

Code. One helper chooses glm() or mgcv::gam(), and gives the formula an environment in which s() and the others are mgcv’s, so users need not attach mgcv:

.fit_glm_or_gam <- function(args) {
  if (.uses_smooths(args$formula)) {
    .require_mgcv()
    args$formula <- .gam_formula(args$formula)
    args$na.action <- NULL
    do.call(mgcv::gam, args)
  } else {
    do.call(stats::glm, args)
  }
}

Why this approach.

  • The problem: a regression assumes each confounder has a straight-line effect (on the logit scale for a yes/no exposure). That is often wrong: the chance of starting treatment may rise steeply at low CD4 counts and then level off. A straight line then gives the wrong probabilities, and some confounding remains in the weighted analysis.
  • The old fix: add splines or polynomials by hand. That means choosing knots or degrees, and it is easy to make the curve too stiff or too wiggly.
  • What a GAM does: writing s(cd4) lets the data decide the shape of the curve, while a penalty keeps it smooth so it does not follow random noise.
  • Why mgcv: it is the standard, well-tested R package for GAMs and is shipped with R as a recommended package, so most users already have it.
  • Why only some families: for binomial, gaussian and Poisson, a GAM is a direct replacement for the GLM already used. Multinomial, ordinal, gamma and negative binomial would need different fitting code, so they are left for later.
  • Tip: use s() for continuous confounders where a curved effect is plausible, and look at plot(result$den.mod) to see the fitted curves.

Implementation note. For gaussian exposures, the GAM uses σ = sqrt(sig2) (residual sum of squares over n minus the effective degrees of freedom), while the GLM path keeps sd(residuals) from earlier versions, so the two are not on exactly the same footing.

5. ipwtm(): type “all” for multinomial and ordinal exposures

Every interval now contributes the probability of the observed category, so the weight follows exposures that move between categories in both directions.

Formula. With categories 1, …, J, the multinomial model is a baseline-category logit; the ordinal model a cumulative link model with link g (logit, probit, cauchit or cloglog):

P(Aik=j∣Lik)=exp⁡(Lik⊤βj)∑m=1Jexp⁡(Lik⊤βm),β1=0 P(A_{ik} = j \mid L_{ik}) = \frac{\exp(L_{ik}^\top \beta_j)}{\sum_{m=1}^{J} \exp(L_{ik}^\top \beta_m)}, \quad \beta_1 = 0

P(Aik≤j∣Lik)=g−1(ζj−Lik⊤β) P(A_{ik} \le j \mid L_{ik}) = g^{-1}(\zeta_j - L_{ik}^\top \beta)

The weight is the time-varying product in the notation section, with f(Aik | ·) the fitted probability of the category observed in interval k.

Code. With type = "all" every row is selected (selvar = 1), so the existing categorical engine fits nnet::multinom() or MASS::polr() on all rows:

p_vec[active] <- .prob_of_observed(stats::predict(mod, type = "probs"),
                                   data[[exp_col]][active], mod$lev)
weights <- unsplit(lapply(split(p_ratio, data[[id_col]]), cumprod), data[[id_col]])

Why this approach.

  • The problem: some exposures change more than once. A patient’s adherence can be high, then low, then high again. With type = "first", ipw stops following a person after their first change, so the later changes are ignored.
  • What it does: every visit counts. At each visit the model asks: given this person’s history, how likely was the category they actually had? These chances are multiplied over time to give the weight.
  • Why this way: it is the method ipw already uses for yes/no exposures with type = "all", extended to more than two categories. The multinomial and ordinal models were already in the package, so little new code was needed.
  • Which model to use: multinomial when the categories have no order (drug A, B or C); ordinal when they do (low, medium, high). The ordinal model uses one effect per covariate instead of one per category, so it needs less data.

Caveat. The models are pooled over time, so the user must put past exposure (for example the previous category) and time in the formulas; the function does not add them.

6. ipwtm(): type “all” for recurrent exposure events (survival)

Exposure events can now happen more than once per person, for example repeated prescriptions or hospital admissions. This follows Graffeo, Latouche, Geskus and Chevret (2018).

Formula. An Andersen–Gill Cox model for the exposure events is fitted on all rows, with baseline cumulative hazard Λ0(t). Row k of person i covers the interval (sik, tik] and has covariates Lik:

P(Aik=0∣Lik)=exp⁡{−[Λ0(tik)−Λ0(sik)]eβ⊤Lik} P(A_{ik} = 0 \mid L_{ik}) = \exp\big\{-\big[\Lambda_0(t_{ik}) - \Lambda_0(s_{ik})\big]\, e^{\beta^\top L_{ik}}\big\}

P(Aik=1∣Lik)=1−P(Aik=0∣Lik) P(A_{ik} = 1 \mid L_{ik}) = 1 - P(A_{ik} = 0 \mid L_{ik})

The weight is the time-varying product in the notation section, with f(Aik | ·) the probability of the status observed in row k (event or no event).

Code. The model is coxph(Surv(tstart, timevar, exposure) ~ ...) on all rows; each row’s probability uses the baseline hazard over that row’s own interval:

bh <- survival::basehaz(mod, centered = TRUE)
d_cum_haz <- cum_haz_at(data[[time_col]]) - cum_haz_at(data[[start_col]])
h <- d_cum_haz * stats::predict(mod, type = "risk", centered = TRUE)
ifelse(data[[exp_col]] == 1, 1 - exp(-h), exp(-h))

Why this approach.

  • The problem: with type = "first", ipw stops following a person after their first exposure event, so later prescriptions or admissions are ignored.
  • What it does: every row counts. For each interval the model asks: given this person’s covariates, how likely was an event (or no event) in this interval? These chances are multiplied over time to give the weight.
  • Why the Andersen–Gill model: it is the standard Cox model for recurrent events and is already in the survival package, so ipw adds only the step from hazard to probability.
  • Why each row’s own interval: in start-stop data cut at events, rows have different lengths for different people. Using Λ0(tik) − Λ0(sik) gives each row the hazard over exactly the time it covers, instead of assuming a shared grid of visits.
  • Simulation check: the Cox coefficients were unbiased, the estimated weights were within 7–9% of the true weights, and the effect of the number of events was recovered with 0.8% bias, against 21% for regression adjustment and 79% unweighted (simulation study, scenarios 6a–6c).

Caveat. For an interval that ends in an event, the method uses the probability of an event at some time during the interval, which is an approximation (Graffeo et al. 2018). The model assumes events are independent given the covariates, so the number of earlier events should be in the formula when it affects the hazard.

7. ipwprobtm(): time-varying weights from user-supplied probabilities

ipwprobtm() separates the weight arithmetic from the modelling: the user brings f from any model, and ipw multiplies the ratios over time within each subject and truncates the weights. It is the last step of ipwtm() without the model fitting.

Formula. With den = f(Aik | ·) and num = f(Aik | ·) from the numerator model, per row (num = 1 when not given), the weight is the cumulative product within each subject, ordered by time, as in the notation section:

Wi(t)=∏k≤tnumikdenik W_i(t) = \prod_{k \le t} \frac{num_{ik}}{den_{ik}}

Code.

ratio <- num / den
ord <- order(id, timevar)
cum <- unsplit(lapply(split(ratio[ord], id[ord]), cumprod), id[ord])
weights <- numeric(n)
weights[ord] <- cum        # back to the user's row order

It checks that den and num are positive and finite, that lengths match, and that each id–time pair occurs once; id and timevar are required.

Why this approach.

  • The problem: ipw only fits regression models. Many analysts now estimate the chance of treatment with machine learning (random forests, boosting, SuperLearner), which can pick up complex patterns a regression misses. Until now they had to compute the weights by hand.
  • What it does: you give, for each row, the probability of the treatment the person actually received. ipw does the rest: divides numerator by denominator, multiplies over time within each person, and truncates if asked.
  • Why this way: building every learner into ipw would add many dependencies and break whenever those packages change. Accepting probabilities works with any method, now and in future, and keeps ipw small.
  • Why time-varying only: for a point treatment the weight is simply num / den, one line of R, so a function adds nothing. For time-varying data the ratios must be multiplied within each person, in time order, and returned in the original row order; that is where mistakes happen.
  • Why it asks for timevar: time-varying weights must be multiplied in time order. Asking for the time, instead of trusting the row order, avoids wrong weights when the data are not sorted.
  • When to use: when you fitted the treatment model yourself, or want to compare several models on the same data.

Caveats. Flexible models can give probabilities near 0 or 1 and so extreme weights; truncation (trunc) and cross-fitting help. The user is responsible for setting probabilities to 1 after the first switch for type = "first" or "cens". Standard errors that ignore the estimation of the probabilities are only approximate.

8. ipwvcov(): standard errors that account for the estimated weights

ipwvcov() (experimental) gives the variance of the coefficients of a marginal structural model fitted with lm(), glm() or coxph() and weights from ipwpoint(family = "binomial"), with the estimation of the weights taken into account (M-estimation: Lunceford & Davidian 2004; Stefanski & Boos 2002).

Formula. Stack the parameters θ=(β,α,γ)\theta = (\beta, \alpha, \gamma) of the MSM, the denominator model and the (optional) numerator model. For person i, with MSM design row XiX_i, mean μi\mu_i, variance function VV, and exposure-model design rows ZiZ_i (denominator, fitted pip_i) and ZinumZ^{num}_i (numerator, fitted qiq_i):

ψi(θ)=(UiSiRi)=(wiXi(yi−μi)dμi/dηiV(μi)Zi(ai−pi)dpi/dηipi(1−pi)Zinum(ai−qi)dqi/dηiqi(1−qi)) \psi_i(\theta) = \begin{pmatrix} U_i \\ S_i \\ R_i \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} w_i X_i (y_i - \mu_i)\, \frac{d\mu_i/d\eta_i}{V(\mu_i)} \\ Z_i (a_i - p_i)\, \frac{dp_i/d\eta_i}{p_i(1-p_i)} \\ Z^{num}_i (a_i - q_i)\, \frac{dq_i/d\eta_i}{q_i(1-q_i)} \end{pmatrix}

Because UiU_i is proportional to wiw_i, ∂Ui/∂α=UidiT\partial U_i / \partial \alpha = U_i d_i^T with di=∂log⁡wi/∂α=g(ai,pi)(dpi/dηi)Zid_i = \partial \log w_i / \partial \alpha = g(a_i, p_i)\, (dp_i/d\eta_i)\, Z_i, where

estimand g(1,p)g(1, p) g(0,p)g(0, p)
ATE −1/p-1/p 1/(1−p)1/(1-p)
ATT 00 1/(p(1−p))1/(p(1-p))
ATC −1/(p(1−p))-1/(p(1-p)) 00
ATO −1/(1−p)-1/(1-p) 1/p1/p

and, for stabilized ATE weights, ei=∂log⁡wi/∂γ=(ai/qi−(1−ai)/(1−qi))(dqi/dηi)Zinume_i = \partial \log w_i / \partial \gamma = (a_i/q_i - (1-a_i)/(1-q_i))\, (dq_i/d\eta_i)\, Z^{num}_i. The bread A=−∑i∂ψi/∂θA = -\sum_i \partial \psi_i / \partial \theta is block upper-triangular:

A=(∑iwi(dμi/dηi)2V(μi)XiXiT−∑iUidiT−∑iUieiT0∑i(dpi/dηi)2pi(1−pi)ZiZiT000∑i(dqi/dηi)2qi(1−qi)ZinumZinumT) A = \begin{pmatrix} \sum_i w_i \frac{(d\mu_i/d\eta_i)^2}{V(\mu_i)} X_i X_i^T & -\sum_i U_i d_i^T & -\sum_i U_i e_i^T \\ 0 & \sum_i \frac{(dp_i/d\eta_i)^2}{p_i(1-p_i)} Z_i Z_i^T & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & \sum_i \frac{(dq_i/d\eta_i)^2}{q_i(1-q_i)} Z^{num}_i Z^{num\,T}_i \end{pmatrix}

the meat is B=∑iψiψiTB = \sum_i \psi_i \psi_i^T, and the variance is A−1BA−TA^{-1} B A^{-T}; ipwvcov() returns its β\beta block.

Code. Each block is a cross-product computed in base R; for example, for the denominator model and the β\beta-α\alpha block:

g <- switch(estimand,
  ATE = ifelse(a == 1, -1 / p, 1 / (1 - p)),
  ATT = ifelse(a == 1, 0, 1 / (p * (1 - p))),
  ATC = ifelse(a == 1, -1 / (p * (1 - p)), 0),
  ATO = ifelse(a == 1, -1 / (1 - p), 1 / p))
D <- den$Z * (g * den$dp)          # rows d_i
A[beta, alpha] <- -crossprod(U, D)
V <- solve(A) %*% crossprod(Psi) %*% t(solve(A))

Why this approach. Robust standard errors of the weighted MSM treat the weights as known. Estimating the weights usually reduces the variance of an ATE estimate, so these standard errors are conservative for the ATE, but for the ATT, ATC and ATO they can be too small. The stacked estimating equations account for this exactly (asymptotically) and need no resampling. The bread uses expected (Fisher) information. For canonical links (logit, gaussian identity) this equals the observed information, so the sandwich is exact; for other links the two are only asymptotically equivalent, and in the tests a probit or cloglog exposure model gave standard errors up to 2% away from the exact (numerical-Jacobian) sandwich. ipwvcov() therefore requires logistic exposure models. For the marginal structural model any glm() link is accepted. For a saturated model such as y ~ a with a binary exposure, the expected and observed information are exactly equal in any sample, whatever the link: the fitted mean in each exposure group is that group’s weighted mean of y, so the extra term of the observed information, ∑iwiXiXiT(yi−μi)c(ηi)\sum_i w_i X_i X_i^T (y_i - \mu_i)\, c(\eta_i) with cc the derivative of (dμ/dη)/V(μ)(d\mu/d\eta)/V(\mu) with respect to η\eta, sums to zero within each group, where ηi\eta_i and hence c(ηi)c(\eta_i) are constant. For other MSMs with a non-canonical link (for example a log link with covariates) the two are asymptotically equivalent when the model is correctly specified. Dispersion parameters cancel. No small-sample correction is applied. The package tests compare the result with a numerical Jacobian of the stacked equations and with glm_weightit(vcov = "asympt") from the WeightIt package.

Cox marginal structural models. For coxph() with right-censored data, one row per person, the estimating equation for β\beta is the weighted partial likelihood score (Binder 1992; Lin & Wei 1989), with the Breslow form for tied event times. With δi\delta_i the event indicator, Yj(t)Y_j(t) the at-risk indicator, S0(t)=∑jwjYj(t)eβTXjS_0(t) = \sum_j w_j Y_j(t) e^{\beta^T X_j}, S1(t)=∑jwjYj(t)eβTXjXjS_1(t) = \sum_j w_j Y_j(t) e^{\beta^T X_j} X_j and X‾(t)=S1(t)/S0(t)\bar X(t) = S_1(t) / S_0(t), person ii’s contribution is

Ui=wi[δi(Xi−X‾(ti))−∑kδkwkYi(tk)eβTXi(Xi−X‾(tk))S0(tk)]=wiri, U_i = w_i \Big[ \delta_i \big(X_i - \bar X(t_i)\big) - \sum_k \frac{\delta_k w_k Y_i(t_k)\, e^{\beta^T X_i} \big(X_i - \bar X(t_k)\big)}{S_0(t_k)} \Big] = w_i\, r_i ,

where rir_i, the score residual, is what residuals(msm, type = "score") returns (without the weight). The bread for β\beta is the weighted information ∑kδkwk[S2(tk)/S0(tk)−X‾(tk)X‾(tk)T]\sum_k \delta_k w_k \big[S_2(t_k)/S_0(t_k) - \bar X(t_k) \bar X(t_k)^T\big], the inverse of msm$naive.var.

The weights appear in each person’s own term and in the risk-set sums S0S_0, S1S_1, so it is not obvious that the cross block keeps the glm form. It does. The total score is ∑kδkwk(Xk−X‾(tk))\sum_k \delta_k w_k (X_k - \bar X(t_k)), and its derivative with respect to one weight wjw_j is

∂∂wj∑iUi=δj(Xj−X‾(tj))−∑kδkwkYj(tk)eβTXj(Xj−X‾(tk))S0(tk)=rj, \frac{\partial}{\partial w_j} \sum_i U_i = \delta_j \big(X_j - \bar X(t_j)\big) - \sum_k \delta_k w_k \frac{Y_j(t_k)\, e^{\beta^T X_j} \big(X_j - \bar X(t_k)\big)}{S_0(t_k)} = r_j ,

because ∂X‾(tk)/∂wj=Yj(tk)eβTXj(Xj−X‾(tk))/S0(tk)\partial \bar X(t_k) / \partial w_j = Y_j(t_k) e^{\beta^T X_j} (X_j - \bar X(t_k)) / S_0(t_k). Hence ∂∑iUi/∂α=∑jrj∂wj/∂αT=∑jUjdjT\partial \sum_i U_i / \partial \alpha = \sum_j r_j\, \partial w_j / \partial \alpha^T = \sum_j U_j d_j^T, the same expression as for glm(), and ipwvcov() computes it analytically. The tests compare the whole variance with central finite differences of the stacked equations, with risk sets computed by brute force; they agree to about 10−710^{-7}. Without the exposure-model blocks the sandwich is I−1∑iUiUiTI−1I^{-1} \sum_i U_i U_i^T I^{-1}, which is exactly coxph()’s robust variance (msm$var): the standard error that treats the weights as known.

With tied event times, Efron’s approximation changes the score and the information in a way that ipw does not reproduce, so ipwvcov() requires ties = "breslow" when event times are tied. Without tied event times all tie methods give the same partial likelihood, and any ties is accepted.

WeightIt::coxph_weightit(vcov = "asympt") gives slightly different values. Its vcov = "HC0" equals coxph()’s robust variance exactly, and the weights agree to 10−1410^{-14}, so the difference lies in how the dependence of the Cox score on the propensity-model coefficients enters. In our checks the relative difference was below 0.1% for ATE and overlap weights and shrank with the sample size; for ATT and ATC weights WeightIt’s standard error was 1 to 4% larger and the difference did not shrink (n from 600 to 38 400). ipwvcov() matches the numerical Jacobian of the exact stacked equations in all cases.

Time-varying weights from ipwtm(). For family = "binomial" with logistic models, each model (denominator, numerator; treatment, censoring) is a parameter block, and the person, not the row, is the unit of independence. For row rr of person pp, ipwtm() defines the weight as a product over that person’s rows s≤rs \le r in time order,

wr=∏s≤rfsnumfsden,fs={P(As=as)type "first" or "all", rows used by the model1−pstype "cens", rows used by the model (the censoring row included)1rows after the first switch ("first", "cens"), w_r = \prod_{s \le r} \frac{f^{num}_s}{f^{den}_s}, \qquad f_s = \begin{cases} P(A_s = a_s) & \text{type "first" or "all", rows used by the model}\\ 1 - p_s & \text{type "cens", rows used by the model (the censoring row included)}\\ 1 & \text{rows after the first switch ("first", "cens")}, \end{cases}

where the rows used by the model are those with selvar = 1 (all rows for type = "all"). With logistic models, ∂log⁡fs/∂α=(as−ps)Zs\partial \log f_s / \partial \alpha = (a_s - p_s) Z_s for “first” and “all”, and −psZs-p_s Z_s for “cens”, so

dr=∂log⁡wr∂α=−∑s≤r,s∈p∂log⁡fsden∂α,er=∂log⁡wr∂γ=∑s≤r,s∈p∂log⁡fsnum∂γ, d_r = \frac{\partial \log w_r}{\partial \alpha} = -\sum_{s \le r,\ s \in p} \frac{\partial \log f^{den}_s}{\partial \alpha}, \qquad e_r = \frac{\partial \log w_r}{\partial \gamma} = \sum_{s \le r,\ s \in p} \frac{\partial \log f^{num}_s}{\partial \gamma},

cumulative sums within person, which also carry the value forward after the switch. The exposure-model score of person pp is Sp=∑s(as−ps)ZsS_p = \sum_s (a_s - p_s) Z_s over the rows used by the model, and its information comes from the fitted glm. For the MSM, UrU_r is the row score (the glm score, or for a Cox model on counting-process data Surv(tstart, time, event) the weighted score residual with risk sets {j:tjstart<t≤tj}\{j: t^{start}_j < t \le t_j\}), the cross blocks are −∑rUrdrT-\sum_r U_r d_r^T and −∑rUrerT-\sum_r U_r e_r^T (for the Cox model by the same identity as above, now row by row), and the meat is B=∑pψpψpTB = \sum_p \psi_p \psi_p^T with ψp\psi_p the sum of all scores of person pp. A list of weight objects whose weights multiply, such as treatment times censoring weights, adds one block per model.

The package tests compare the result with central finite differences of the stacked equations, with the weights recomputed from the model coefficients by independent code that follows the definition above (agreement about 10−710^{-7}, on shuffled rows), for a glm() MSM with “all” and “cens” weights, a Cox MSM with “first” and “cens” weights and a subset of haartdat. They also compare with WeightIt::glm_weightit(vcov = "asympt") for a weightitMSM() object: with visits at the same times for everyone and time-specific columns in the pooled model, the weights are the same, and an MSM fitted on the long data with one parameter per non-last row (so that only the last rows carry information) has the same coefficients and variance as WeightIt’s person-level model (agreement 10−610^{-6}).

Heavy-tailed weights. Cumulative weights are products of many factors. When some people have a very low probability of their observed exposure history (a near-violation of positivity), the weights have a heavy right tail: P(W > x) falls off like x−γx^{-\gamma} for a tail index γ\gamma. The weighted estimating equations then have a finite variance only if γ>2\gamma > 2. The usual normal approximation also relies on a finite third moment (γ>3\gamma > 3), and estimating the variance well, from the sandwich or from the bootstrap, relies on a finite fourth moment (γ>4\gamma > 4).

Simulations with individual visit times (see the comparison article) estimated γ\gamma with the Hill estimator on the top 5% of the final cumulative weights. The more strongly treatment depended on the confounder and on the previous treatment, the smaller the tail index: about 3.9, 2.8 and 2.3 in three scenarios. Coverage of 95% intervals from ipwvcov() followed the tail index: 95.8%, 93.4 to 94.6% and 91.6 to 93.2%. On the variance scale, the mean estimated variance from ipwvcov() was 1.05 times the empirical variance of the estimates in the moderate scenario, but 0.89 to 0.90 and 0.84 to 0.93 times it in the two heavy-tailed ones (relative error in the model-based standard error -8 to -3%, MCSE 2 to 4 points). Neither the variance ratio nor the coverage improved between 300 and 4800 people, while the largest weight kept growing with n. The cluster bootstrap did no better: its variance ratio was 0.81 to 1.00, but on 100 to 200 data sets this is too imprecise (MCSE of the relative error 2 to 12 points) to tell it apart from ipwvcov(). The formula is exact for the stacked estimating equations; the problem is the weights, and it affects any normal-theory interval. Check the weight distribution (summary(), ipwplot(), the effective sample size) before trusting any standard error. If a few people carry much of the weight, consider truncation, a less extreme weight model or a different estimand.

Caveats. Only binary exposures with logistic glm() exposure models; truncated weights (truncation at estimated percentiles is not a smooth function of α\alpha), smooth terms, other families (including Cox exposure models in ipwtm(family = "survival")), Cox MSMs with strata or frailties, and Efron ties with tied event times are not covered, and the bootstrap remains the advice there.

How the simulations judge a standard error

The main vignette and the comparison article say that, in a simulation, ipwvcov() gave correct standard errors and the robust standard error did not. This section explains how such a simulation works and how to read its numbers, following Morris, White & Crowther (2019). The example is the Cox simulation of the comparison article (section “A Cox outcome model”).

What a simulation does. We set up a world in which the true effect is known: how the confounder is generated, how treatment depends on it and how the outcome depends on both. Then we repeat the same study on many data sets, here 1000 data sets of 500 people. In each data set we estimate the effect as in a real analysis and compute its robust and its ipwvcov() standard error.

The true variability. The estimate changes from one data set to the next. The variance of the estimates across the data sets (the empirical variance) is the true variance of the estimator, and its square root (the empirical SE) is the true standard error. A real study cannot measure them, because it has only one data set. A standard error from one data set tries to estimate the empirical SE.

Why variances, not standard errors, are compared. ipwvcov(), like other sandwich formulas, estimates a variance, and a good variance estimator is unbiased: on average across data sets, the estimated variance SE² equals the empirical variance. The standard error is its square root, and the average of square roots is smaller than the square root of the average (Jensen’s inequality). So even for a correct variance estimator the mean SE comes out a little smaller than the empirical SE, more so the more the SE varies between data sets. (Here the mean ipwvcov() SE for the ATE is 0.11% below the square root of the mean SE², a small but avoidable distortion.) The simulations therefore compare the mean estimated variance, mean(SE²), with the empirical variance, var(estimate), and report their ratio (1 is ideal). For readability they also give the model-based SE, sqrt(mean(SE²)), next to the empirical SE, and the relative error in the model-based SE, 100 × (model SE / empirical SE − 1), as in Table 6 of Morris et al.

In the Cox simulation the empirical variance of the log hazard ratio was 0.0164 for the ATE (empirical SE 0.128) and 0.0176 for overlap weights (ATO; SE 0.133). For ipwvcov() the variance ratio was 0.998 and 0.996: the model-based SE was 0.128 and 0.132, a relative error of -0.1% (MCSE 2.2) and -0.2% (MCSE 2.2). For the robust standard error the variance ratio was 1.200 and 1.115 (model-based SE 0.140 and 0.140, relative error +9.6% (MCSE 2.5) and +5.6% (MCSE 2.4)): its variance is too large.

How precise that is. The empirical variance is itself estimated from a finite number of data sets. With R data sets its relative Monte Carlo standard error (MCSE) is about sqrt(2 / (R − 1)), which is 4.5% for R = 1000; on the SE scale this halves, to about 2.2%. The MCSE of the relative error in the model-based SE (in brackets above) adds the variability of the estimated variances themselves (Morris et al., Table 6). A relative error of under 1% for ipwvcov(), with an MCSE above 2%, is no detectable difference. For the robust standard error, the relative error is about 3.9 MCSEs from 0 for the ATE and 2.4 for the ATO: a real difference.

Coverage, an independent check. Because the true effect is known, we can count how often the 95% interval (estimate ± 1.96 × SE) contains it. This check does not use the empirical variance at all. Coverage is also estimated from a finite number of data sets: for a coverage p, its MCSE is sqrt(p(1 − p) / R), about 0.7 percentage points near 95% for R = 1000 and 1.3 for R = 300 (the number of data sets with a bootstrap). Intervals that are too wide cover the truth more often than 95%, and correct ones about 95% of the time. The robust intervals covered it in 96.9% (ATE) and 96.1% (ATO) of the data sets, the ipwvcov() intervals in 95.6% and 95.6%.

Why the truth is the marginal log hazard ratio. The data are simulated from a model given the confounder, with a conditional hazard ratio of exp(-0.5) for treatment. The MSM, a Cox model with treatment only, targets something else: the marginal hazard ratio, which compares the whole target population treated with the whole population untreated. For hazard ratios the two differ even without confounding (hazard ratios are not collapsible), and the marginal one is closer to 1. So the truth is computed directly. For every person in a very large simulated sample, both potential survival times (treated and untreated) are generated, and a Cox model of time on treatment is fitted to these data (for the ATO weighted by e(1 − e), with e the propensity score). This gives a true log hazard ratio of NA for the ATE and NA for the ATO, not -0.5. Counting how often the intervals contain -0.5 would wrongly count correct intervals as misses.
